title: De novo assembly of a cancer genome using 3D chromatin data
summary: Assembling a personal cancer genome from ultra-high-resolution chromatin data, with no reference genome used: the first attempt to test this particular technique for genome assembly.
context: Competitive summer research bursary, Institute of Cancer Research

sections.heading: The problem
body: Most cancer genomics compares a tumour's DNA against a single standard reference genome. That works for a normal genome, but cancer genomes are often heavily restructured.
list: The cell line here is HT-29, colorectal cancer, and hypertriploid, with a modal chromosome number of 71 against a normal 46
Forcing that onto a reference built for a normal genome loses real structural information, and GRCh38 carries its own biases: it is largely one individual, 70% of it a single male
The alternative is de novo assembly: building the genome from the cell's own sequencing data, with no reference at all

sections.heading: Approach
body: Whole-genome sequencing combined with Micro-C, a newer variant of Hi-C with a much better signal-to-noise ratio for short-range chromatin contacts. Both capture which regions of DNA sit physically close together in the nucleus: the signal scaffolding tools use to order fragments into chromosomes. No published study had used Micro-C for assembly before, so part of the question was simply whether the extra resolution helps.
list: Three scaffolders ran in parallel on the same draft assembly, on the institute's HPC cluster: 3d-dna, HapHiC and Puzzle Hi-C

Only 3d-dna completed. HapHiC and Puzzle Hi-C both hung during multiprocessing, an incompatibility between their Python multiprocessing implementations and the cluster's memory limits, not a flaw in the underlying method
Juicer's explicit memory allocation threw persistent SLURM errors. Adapting its scripts to the institute's cluster fixed it, and left them reusable for other projects

Of the four pipelines, only Puzzle Hi-C had no checkpointing, so every crash meant restarting from scratch. I patched the local code to add a save point after initial file creation, purely to make debugging survivable

body: Three constraints shaped what the working pipeline could actually be given.
list: 3d-dna ignores contigs under 15,000bp by default. The first contact map came out accurate only in its top-left corner until the draft assembly and the paired-contacts file were both filtered to match
All nine Micro-C reads together exceeded the maximum memory available on the cluster, so only the two best reads made it into the final run, which may itself have cost accuracy
Five rounds of scaffolding, each one measurably better than the last, which suggests the assembly was still improving when the rounds stopped

sections.heading: Result
list: 25 chromosome-scale scaffolds recovered, with no reference genome used to build them
Manual review in JuiceBox caught real errors the automated pipeline alone would have missed: a translocation in chromosome 15, and inversions in chromosomes 13, 14, 24 and 25, all corrected by hand

images.caption: Straight out of 3d-dna. Blue squares are identified chromosomes; the off-diagonal signal breaking away from the diagonal is the kind of misjoin manual review exists to catch.

images.alt: Contact map of the same assembly after manual curation in JBAT, with the off-diagonal signal resolved and contact intensity following the diagonal through the scaffold boundaries

sections.heading: Effect of Micro-C resolution
body: This had a clear answer, and it ran the opposite way from what I expected.
list: Micro-C's advantage is short-range detail, and that is exactly what caused problems here
At native resolution it produced far more small scaffolds than the tool was built to handle
Those scaffolds were visible only at 5kb zoom, too fine to compare against other regions, so no further manual adjustment could be made
3d-dna is tuned for standard Hi-C resolution. The extra detail worked against the tool's own assumptions rather than helping

images.alt: Contact map zoomed to 5kb resolution across a roughly 400kb window, showing a long run of small green Micro-C scaffold boxes along the diagonal
images.caption: The same assembly at 5kb zoom. Green squares are Micro-C scaffolds: a 400kb window carrying a whole run of them, with nothing else in view to compare against.

sections.heading: Reference-based validation
body: The assembly used no reference, but evaluating it needed one: the finished scaffolds were aligned to GRCh38 with LASTZ. That check didn't resolve either.
list: The alignments ran to roughly 300GB, past what the available memory could plot
Only chromosome 21, the smallest result, could be filtered down far enough to visualise

A correct assembly should show a clean diagonal against its reference chromosome. This one showed no clear synteny, so the comparison stayed inconclusive rather than confirming or refuting the assembly
